newsitem.title: USA: Documents questions on postwar Swiss bank dealings.
newsitem.headline: Documents questions on postwar Swiss bank dealings.

text.p: A postwar U.S. intelligence document accuses Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS), involved in a document-shredding incident earlier this year, of possibly violating a 1946 U.S.-Swiss treaty in its dealings with a German bank, researchers said on Thursday.

A 1947 U.S. military government document said that Union Bank and the German Eidgenoessische bank "have attempted to set off German balances against Swiss claims in Switzerland, which is possibly in violation of the Allied-Swiss accord."

The document, found by researchers for the World Jewish Congress, said there were transfers of several hundred thousand Swiss francs between the two banks in 1947. The U.S.-Swiss accord required Switzerland to return looted Nazi gold and liquidate German assets in Switzerland.

Union Bank took over Eidgenoessische Bank after the war and last January it sparked a major controversy when a young Swiss bank guard discovered it illegally shredding some of the German bank's Nazi-era documents and ledgers.
Earlier this week, the guard, Christoph Meili, was granted emergency residency status in the United States by President Bill Clinton after Meili said he received death threats at home.

World Jewish Congress Vice President Kalman Sultanik said the document found in the U.S. National Archives was turned over to New York Sen. Alfonse D'Amato, Republican chairman of the Senate Banking Committee, who on Wednesday threatened sanctions against Union Bank unless Meili received an apology.
"Senator D'Amato is championing the righteous cause of Christoph Meili who has stirred the American conscience and defended the honour of Switzerland," Sultanik said.
Meili was fired after he reported the shredding incident and threatened with arrest for stealing bank documents.
Sultanik said the newly discovered document raised new questions about the shredding incident because it charges that the two banks had extensive postwar dealings that provoked U.S. suspicions.
Union Bank has called the shredding routine but this week it said that three documents were possibly related to the forced sale of Jewish property in Berlin.
